name: Abraham
title: Father of Faith and Covenant Founder
summary: Abraham is the ancestor of God's covenant people and the foremost example of faith in the biblical narrative. God called him out from Ur of the Chaldeans to leave and journey toward an unknown land, with the promise that all peoples on earth would be blessed through his offspring (Gen 12:1-3). Through several covenants – the covenant of sacrifice where God alone took upon himself the obligation (Gen 15), the covenant of circumcision which gave the outward sign of the covenant (Gen 17), and the renewed oath at Moriah (Gen 22:15-18) – Abraham became a bearer of a salvation promise that ties together all Scripture, from Israel's founding to the Messiah. His life testifies to bold obedience and human weakness: he left everything on God's word, but also tried to secure the fulfillment of the promise by his own means, as with Hagar (Gen 16). He is the only one in the Old Testament called "God's friend" (Isa 41:8; 2 Chr 20:7; Jas 2:23), and the apostles present him as the pattern of faith for all peoples (Rom 4; Gal 3:6-9; Heb 11:8-19). The Gospel of Matthew opens by calling Jesus "son of Abraham" (Matt 1:1), thus marking that the covenant promises to Abraham find their final fulfillment in Christ. Abraham's willingness to offer Isaac on Mount Moriah stands as one of Scripture's strongest examples of God's own sacrifice, and his life as a stranger and pilgrim in the land of promise (Gen 23:4; Heb 11:13) has shaped the biblical understanding of faith's journey.

keyEvents.title: The Call from God
keyEvents.description: God called Abram to leave Ur and go to a land he would show him, with the promise of blessing, a great name, and that all families of the earth would be blessed through him.

keyEvents.title: Victory over the Kings and the Meeting with Melchizedek
keyEvents.description: Abraham defeated a coalition of kings to free his nephew Lot, and was then blessed by Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High. Abraham gave him a tenth of everything.

keyEvents.title: The Covenant Between the Pieces
keyEvents.description: God made a solemn covenant with Abraham, promising him descendants as numerous as the stars and land from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates. Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.

keyEvents.title: The Covenant and Circumcision
keyEvents.description: God established his eternal covenant with Abraham, changed his name from Abram to Abraham, and gave circumcision as the outward sign of the covenant.

keyEvents.title: The Visit at the Oaks of Mamre
keyEvents.description: Three men visited Abraham at Mamre, and the Lord himself revealed that Sarah would bear a son within a year. Sarah laughed when she heard this, but God confirmed his promise.

keyEvents.title: Intercession for Sodom
keyEvents.description: Abraham interceded for Sodom and negotiated with God to spare the city if there were righteous people there, all the way down to ten.

keyEvents.title: The Birth of Isaac
keyEvents.description: Sarah gave birth to Isaac when Abraham was one hundred years old – a miraculous fulfillment of God's promise given many years earlier.

keyEvents.title: The Test of Faith – Akeda
keyEvents.description: God tested Abraham by asking him to sacrifice his son Isaac on Mount Moriah. Abraham obeyed in faith, but God stopped him and provided a ram as a substitute offering. The event confirmed Abraham's reverence for God and triggered a renewed blessing.

keyEvents.title: Sarah's Death and the Purchase of the Cave of Machpelah
keyEvents.description: After Sarah's death, Abraham bought the Cave of Machpelah in Hebron from the Hittite Ephron as a burial site. This was the first piece of land Abraham owned in the promised land, and it became the family's burial place.

versions.summary: Abraham is the father of faith and one of the most central figures in the Bible. God called him out from Ur of the Chaldeans and promised that all families of the earth would be blessed through him. His life stands as an example of faith, obedience, and waiting on God's promises.
versions.title: Father of Faith
versions.reason: [minor] Abraham is referred to in Genesis 23:6 as a 'prince of God' and was also a wealthy nomadic chieftain and military leader (Gen 14). The role of 'chieftain' or 'patriarch' could have been included for completeness. In addition, Gen 20:7 explicitly confirms his role as a prophet.; [minor] Abraham also had sons with Keturah after Sarah's death (Gen 25:1-4): Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah. These are not included in the list. For a more complete profile, at least the most important ones should be mentioned.; [minor] Abraham also had Hagar as a secondary wife/concubine (Gen 16:3) and Keturah as a wife/secondary wife after Sarah's death (Gen 25:1). For completeness, these could have been mentioned.; [minor] Several important events are missing, such as Abram's victory over the kings and his meeting with Melchizedek (Gen 14), God's covenant with Abraham between the sacrificed animals (Gen 15:7-21), the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah and Abraham's intercession (Gen 18-19), as well as the name change from Abram to Abraham (Gen 17:5).; [major] The profile completely lacks footnotes. Historical, archaeological, linguistic and theological notes that enrich the understanding of Abraham should be added.; [minor] The dating 'c. 2000-1825 BC' gives a lifespan of 175 years, which agrees with Gen 25:7. Some scholars place Abraham somewhat later (c. 1950-1775 BC), but this is uncertain and the given dating falls within an acceptable range.

versions.summary: Abraham is the father of faith and one of the Bible's most central figures. God called him out from Ur in Chaldea and promised that all families of the earth would be blessed through him (Gen 12:1-3). Through a series of covenant agreements, he became the ancestor of Israel's people and bearer of God's promise of salvation. His life is marked by faith, obedience, and patient waiting for God's promises – but also by human weakness and doubt. Abraham is the only person in the Old Testament who is called "God's friend" (Isa 41:8), and his faith is held up in the New Testament as a pattern for all believers (Rom 4; Gal 3:6-9; Heb 11:8-19).

versions.summary: Abraham is regarded as the father of God's covenant people and stands as a model of faith throughout the biblical narrative. From Ur of the Chaldeans, he was called by God to leave his home and journey toward an unknown land, with the promise that all nations on earth would be blessed through his offspring (Gen 12:1-3). Through repeated covenants – including the covenant of sacrifice (Gen 15) and the covenant of circumcision (Gen 17) – he became a bearer of a salvation promise that extends from Israel's founding to its fulfillment in the New Testament. Abraham's life contains both bold obedience and human weakness: he left everything on God's word, yet also tried to secure his future by his own means. He is the only one in the Old Testament called "God's friend" (Isa 41:8; 2 Chr 20:7), and the apostles present him as the pattern of faith for all nations (Rom 4; Gal 3:6-9; Heb 11:8-19). His willingness to offer Isaac on Mount Moriah stands as one of Scripture's strongest examples of God's own sacrifice.

footnotes.text: The name 'Abram' (אַבְרָם) means 'exalted father', while 'Abraham' (אַבְרָהָם) is traditionally understood as 'father of many nations' (Gen 17:5). The linguistic change marks God's expansion of the covenant promise.

Ur of the Chaldeans, Abraham's hometown, is identified with Tell el-Muqayyar in southern Iraq. Archaeological excavations led by Leonard Woolley (1922–1934) uncovered an advanced Sumerian urban civilization with sophisticated architecture, legal systems, and religious practices, providing context for Abraham's cultural background.

Abraham's journey from Ur through Haran to Canaan reflects known trade routes of the Bronze Age. Texts from Mari and Nuzi (c. 1800–1500 BC) contain parallels to patriarchal customs, including adoption practices, concubinage, and property transfers.

In Jewish tradition (Midrash and Talmud), Abraham is regarded as the first to recognize the one God. According to rabbinic literature (including Genesis Rabbah), Abraham smashed his father's idols when he was young – a story not found in the biblical writings but which highlights his role as a pioneer of monotheism.

Abraham's willingness to sacrifice Isaac (Akeda, 'the binding') is a central theme in both Jewish and Christian theology. In Christian tradition, the event is seen as a type (typology) of God's offering of His own Son. Hebrews 11:17–19 interprets Abraham's faith as believing that God could raise Isaac from the dead.

Abraham is called 'friend of God' in Isaiah 41:8, 2 Chronicles 20:7, and James 2:23. This title is unique in the biblical writings and underscores the close, personal covenant relationship between God and Abraham. In Islamic tradition as well, he bears the title 'Khalil Allah' (Friend of God).

Melchizedek, king of Salem who blessed Abraham (Gen 14:18–20), is a mysterious figure appearing without genealogy. Psalm 110:4 links the coming messianic priesthood to "the order of Melchizedek", and Hebrews 7 elaborates on this as a type of Christ as eternal high priest.

The covenant ritual in Genesis 15, where God alone passed between the divided animals, was a known custom in the ancient Near East. Parallels exist in Hittite and Assyrian treaties, where the passing party assumed the obligation – highlighting that God's covenant with Abraham was unilateral and unconditional.

The Cave of Machpelah in Hebron, which Abraham purchased from the Hittite Ephron as a burial place for Sarah (Genesis 23), is one of the oldest known property transactions in literary history. The site is still honored today by Jews, Christians, and Muslims, and the massive building over the cave was constructed during Herodian times.

The dating of Abraham is debated. Traditional biblical chronology places him around 2000–1800 BC based on genealogies in Genesis and 1 Kings 6:1. Some scholars argue for a later date (c. 1800–1600 BC) based on archaeological and cultural indicators from the Middle Bronze Age in Canaan.
